title: Do Ostriches Bury Their Heads? A 2,000-Year-Old Myth
description:
Do ostriches really bury their heads in the sand? No: the myth goes back to Pliny the Elder about 2,000 years ago, and it likely comes from ostriches lowering their heads to turn their eggs in a shallow ground nest, or lying flat with their necks along the ground to hide from danger.

topic: Why don't ostriches really bury their heads in sand?
script:
Ostriches never bury their heads in sand,
but you've seen it happen. Why?
Blame a Roman writer, Pliny the Elder,
nearly two thousand years ago.
He wrote that ostriches hide their heads in bushes
and think nobody can see them.
Here's what's really going on.
Ostriches dig a shallow hole in the ground
and lay their giant eggs inside.
Several times a day, mom and dad dip their heads down
and roll each egg with their beak.
From far away, the head vanishes.
And if danger's close and they can't get away,
they flop flat, neck stretched along the dirt,
like a big lumpy bush.
But mostly? They just run.
Up to seventy kilometers an hour,
the fastest bird on two legs.
So next time an ostrich looks like it's hiding,
what's it really doing?
key_facts: Ostriches do not bury their heads in sand
The myth is thought to come from Roman naturalist Pliny the Elder around 2,000 years ago (Natural History, Book 10), who wrote that they hide their head and neck in a bush
Ostriches dig shallow holes in the ground to lay their eggs
Both parents rotate the eggs with their beaks several times a day
If they can't escape, they may lie very flat with their necks extended along the ground to blend in
When in danger they often run away, at up to about 70 km/h (43 mph)
The ostrich is the fastest-running bird
